L0: cite0†iframe†www.googletagmanager.com L1: # Authorization Through External Client Apps or Connected Apps and OAuth 2.0
L2: 
L3: For a client application to access REST API resources, it must be authorized as a safe visitor. To implement this authorization, use either an external client app or a connected app and an OAuth 2.0 authorization flow.
L4: Creating connected apps is restricted as of Spring ‘26. You can continue to use existing connected apps during and after Spring ‘26. However, we recommend using cite1†external client apps†help.salesforce.com instead. If you must continue creating connected apps, contact Salesforce Support.
L5: 
L6: See cite2†New connected apps can no longer be created in Spring ‘26†help.salesforce.com for more details.
L7: Both external client apps and connected apps request access to REST API resources on behalf of the client application. For an external client app or connected app to request access, it must be integrated with your org’s REST API using the OAuth 2.0 protocol. OAuth 2.0 is an open protocol that authorizes secure data sharing between applications through the exchange of tokens.
L8: For instructions to configure an external client app, see cite3†Create an External Client App†help.salesforce.com or cite4†Enable OAuth Settings for API Integration†help.salesforce.com in Salesforce Help. For more information about connected apps, see cite5†Connected Apps†help.salesforce.com in Salesforce Help.
L9: OAuth authorization flows grant a client app restricted access to REST API resources on a resource server. Each OAuth flow offers a different process for approving access to a client application, but in general the flows consist of three main steps.
L10:   1. To initiate an authorization flow, a connected app on behalf of a client app requests access to a REST API resource.
L11:   2. In response, an authorizing server grants access tokens to the external client app or connected app.
L12:   3. A resource server validates these access tokens and approves access to the protected REST API resource.
L13: After reviewing and selecting an OAuth authorization flow, apply it to your external client app or connected app. For details about each supported flow, see cite6†OAuth Authorization Flows†help.salesforce.com in Salesforce Help.
L14: 
L15: Salesforce offers the following resources to help you navigate connected apps and OAuth:
L16:   * Salesforce Help: cite1†External Client Apps†help.salesforce.com L17:   * Salesforce Help: cite7†Authorize Apps with OAuth†help.salesforce.com L18:   * Salesforce Help: cite8†OpenID Connect Token Introspection†help.salesforce.com L19:   * Trailhead: cite9†Build Integrations Using External Client Apps†trailhead.salesforce.com --------------------------------------------------------------------------------

L0: cite0†iframe†www.googletagmanager.com L1: # Supported Editions and Required Permissions
L2: 
L3: To access your Salesforce org and data using the Salesforce API, you need both an org and a user with API access enabled. There’s more than one Salesforce Edition that supports API access and multiple ways to grant API permission to a user.
L4: API access is enabled by default in Enterprise, Performance, Unlimited, and Developer Edition orgs. Professional Edition orgs can add API access as an add-on. For more information, visit cite1†Salesforce Help: Add Products and Licenses with the Your Account App†help.salesforce.com or contact a Salesforce account executive.
L5: 
L6: If you send an API request to an org without API access, Salesforce returns a `API_DISABLED_FOR_ORG` error.
L7: To protect the configuration and live data in your production org, we recommend using an isolated environment for active development and testing, such as aDeveloper Edition org, sandbox, or scratch org. When ready, you can move successful changes into your production org.
L8: To make any API call, a user must have the API Enabled permission turned on in the user profile they’re assigned. This permission is enabled by default on some profiles, including many profiles available in Developer Edition orgs. In supported editions, you can also use the Salesforce Integration user license to grant system-to-system integration users full org access while limiting them to API-only operations.
L9: For more information, see Salesforce Help: cite2†Give Integration Users API Only Access†help.salesforce.com L10: See Also

L91: # Authenticating requests
L92: 
L93: How to generate access tokens and make requests
L94: 
L95: Copy page Copy page
L96: 
L97: In order to make requests to the Attio REST API, you need to generate an access token. There are two ways to generate an access token:
L98:   1. By implementing an OAuth 2.0 flow
L99:   2. By generating an API key for your workspace
L100: You should prefer the OAuth 2.0 flow if building an app for multiple workspaces. If you are building an app for a single workspace, you can manually generate an API key to make requests on behalf of that workspace only.
L101: ##
L102: 
L103: cite31†​ L104: 
L105: Generating access tokens
L106: 
L107: ###
L108: 
L109: cite32†​ L110: 
L111: OAuth 2.0
L112: 
L113: Attio implements the standard cite33†OAuth 2.0 specification†datatracker.ietf.org . You can find the reference for our OAuth authorize, token exchange and introspect endpoints cite34†here . If you would prefer a tutorial on how to implement an OAuth 2.0 flow into an existing app, you can find one cite11†here .
L114: ###
L115: 
L116: cite35†​ L117: 
L118: API key
L119: 
L120: If you only need a token for a single workspace, you can generate an API key in the developer settings page of your apps. You can find docs on to do this cite36†here†attio.com .
L121: ##
L122: 
L123: cite37†​ L124: 
L125: Using tokens
L126: 
L127: Both OAuth access tokens and single-workspace access token are used in the same way. Pass the value of the token in the `Authorization` header of your requests like so.
L128: 
L129:     `Authorization: Bearer <access_token>
L130:     `
L131: 
L132: We also support cite38†HTTP Basic Authentication†developer.mozilla.org , where the username is the token and the password is left blank. However, we recommend using Bearer authentication where possible.
L133: ###
L134: 
L135: cite39†​ L136: 
L137: Scopes
L138: Both OAuth access tokens and single-workspace access tokens use scopes to control the resources that the token has access to and the actions that can be performed on those resources. The possible scopes for OAuth and single-workspace access tokens are the same. The reference documentation for each endpoint includes a “Required scopes” section that lists the scopes needed to call that endpoint.
L139: When using an OAuth access token, the scopes are specified by configuring the scope settings for your app in the cite3†Developer console†build.attio.com . When using a single-workspace access token, the scopes are specified in the settings UI when generating the token. Scopes for single-workspace access tokens can also be modified on existing tokens.
